promptText: What is a model's context window, and what unit is it measured in?
options: The number of chat messages a UI displays on screen, measured in messages
The maximum amount of input plus output a model can process in a single call, measured in tokens
The amount of disk space allocated to store conversation logs, measured in megabytes
The number of seconds a model is allowed to spend generating a response
explanation: A context window is a fixed, finite token budget shared between everything sent to the model and everything it generates back; it is measured strictly in the model's own tokenizer units, not words, characters, or messages.

promptText: Why is a context window better compared to a fixed-size arena allocator than to a resizable ArrayList?
options: Because context windows are always exactly 1024 tokens, matching a common array size
Because you get one contiguous block of known, fixed capacity at the start of the call, with no 'expand and copy' operation available mid-call if content doesn't fit
Because ArrayLists cannot hold text data of any kind
Because arena allocators are always faster than any other memory management scheme
explanation: Everything sent to the model must be laid out inside one fixed-capacity block before the call begins; unlike a growable collection, there is no way to expand the window mid-call if content doesn't fit -- it simply does not go in.

promptText: What is the 'lost in the middle' effect?
options: A bug where models randomly delete tokens from the middle of long documents before processing them
The phenomenon where models retrieve and use information near the beginning or end of a long context more reliably than information placed in the middle, even when everything technically fits
A limitation where models can only process the first half of any document longer than the context window
An error that occurs when a conversation has an even number of turns
explanation: Even when relevant information is well within the advertised context length, models show measurably lower retrieval accuracy for content buried in the middle of a long context compared to content near the start or end -- a structural property of how attention behaves, not a bug that can be simply patched.

promptText: Why must an application reserve output tokens before calculating how much input it can send?
options: Output tokens are billed at a completely different currency than input tokens
Input and output share the exact same total token budget; filling the window entirely with input risks leaving too little room for a complete answer, causing responses to get cut off mid-sentence
Reserving output tokens is only necessary for models older than GPT-2
The model automatically expands its context window if output space runs low
explanation: Because input and output tokens draw from the same fixed budget, an application that fills the window with input before checking remaining room can leave insufficient space for the model's response, producing an ugly, silent truncation failure mode.

promptText: What is prompt caching, in plain terms?
options: Storing the entire conversation history in a local database for later analysis
Reusing a provider's already-computed processing of a stable, identical text prefix (like a fixed system prompt) across repeated calls, avoiding redundant computation
A technique for compressing user messages into shorter strings before sending them
A method for predicting what the user will type next based on past prompts
explanation: Prompt caching lets a provider reuse internal computation for text it has already processed, as long as it reappears as an identical prefix at the start of a new request -- stable content like system prompts and tool definitions are the natural candidates.

promptText: Why do tool/function definitions consume context budget even on requests where the model doesn't call any tool?
options: Tool definitions are cached separately and never count against the token budget
Tool definitions must be included in the input on every call so the model knows what's available, so they are tokenized and sent regardless of whether a tool ends up being invoked
Tool definitions only consume tokens if the model decides to use them
Tool definitions are automatically stripped from the prompt if unused
explanation: Tool schemas have to be present in the input for the model to know what tools exist and how to call them, so they are tokenized and billed on every request regardless of whether the model actually invokes a tool in its response.

promptText: A stakeholder proposes solving all context-management problems by switching to a 1-million-token context model and stuffing everything in. What is the strongest technical objection?
options: 1-million-token models do not actually exist, so the proposal is technically impossible

A larger window doesn't eliminate the 'lost in the middle' effect, and prefill cost scales roughly quadratically with input length, so filling a huge window on every call is far slower and more expensive than a well-curated, budgeted context
Larger context windows always produce lower-quality output regardless of content
Context windows above 100,000 tokens are not supported by any tokenizer
explanation: A bigger nominal window raises the ceiling on what fits but does not guarantee correctness (lost-in-the-middle persists) or efficiency (attention cost grows roughly quadratically with sequence length), so disciplined retrieval, ranking, and summarization remain necessary regardless of window size.

promptText: What is a KV cache, and why does its memory footprint matter for production serving at long context lengths?
options: It stores a copy of every user's password to speed up authentication and has no relation to context length

It caches the key and value projections for tokens already processed so each new token only needs fresh computation against the cache; its memory grows with both sequence length and batch size, so it can become the dominant consumer of GPU memory and limit serving concurrency
It is a disk-based cache that stores entire conversation transcripts to avoid re-sending them
It only matters for training, never for inference-time serving
explanation: The KV cache avoids recomputing attention over the whole sequence for every new output token, but because it grows with both sequence length and concurrent batch size, it frequently becomes the binding constraint on how many long-context requests a system can serve simultaneously, ahead of raw compute limits.

promptText: Why does self-attention make the context window a hard architectural wall rather than a soft, gracefully-degrading limit (unlike the leaky memory of older RNN/LSTM models)?
options: Self-attention was deliberately designed to punish long inputs with worse output quality

The attention matrices and computation are sized for a specific maximum sequence length trained into the model; feeding more tokens than that has no well-defined computation to fall back to, so providers return an explicit error rather than a degraded answer
RNNs and Transformers use the exact same memory mechanism, so there is no real difference
Self-attention only works on inputs shorter than 100 tokens by design
explanation: Unlike RNNs, whose fixed-size hidden state degraded gradually (vanishing gradients) with no hard limit, self-attention's all-pairs computation is architecturally sized for a maximum sequence length; exceeding it has no defined fallback, which is why exceeding a Transformer's context length produces a hard error instead of gracefully degraded output.

promptText: Given the 'lost in the middle' effect, where should a non-negotiable system instruction and the single most decision-relevant retrieved document be placed in an assembled prompt?
options: Both should be placed exactly in the middle of the context to balance attention evenly

The system instruction should sit at the very start (a reliably high-attention zone), and the most decision-relevant retrieved content should sit at the very end, right before the user's question (the other reliably high-attention zone)
Order does not matter at all as long as everything fits within the context window
Both should be placed at the very end, immediately after each other, regardless of content type
explanation: Because attention is least reliable in the middle of a long context, critical system instructions belong at the start and the most decisive retrieved content belongs at the end just before the question, while less-critical background material is the right candidate for the middle position, where being partially ignored does the least damage.

promptText: Does a larger context window make Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) obsolete?
options: Yes, once a window is large enough to hold an entire knowledge base, retrieval is no longer needed

No -- RAG's job is selecting the small relevant subset from a knowledge base that is typically far larger than any window; a bigger window changes the economics (larger chunks, higher top-K) but does not remove the need for retrieval
Yes, because larger windows eliminate the 'lost in the middle' effect entirely
No, but only because larger windows are always more expensive to use than smaller ones
explanation: Most real knowledge bases (full documentation, codebases, legal corpora) vastly exceed even a million-token window, so something still has to decide what to include; a bigger window affords larger chunks and higher top-K before re-ranking, but retrieval and ranking discipline remain necessary.

promptText: What invalidates a cached prompt prefix under typical provider-side prompt caching?
options: Nothing invalidates it; once cached, a prefix stays valid forever regardless of changes

Any change earlier in the sequence than the cached portion -- even a single-character edit to the system prompt, a reordered tool definition, or inserting a timestamp before the stable content -- since the cache is keyed on exact prefix match, not semantic similarity
Only changing the model version invalidates the cache; content changes never do
Caches are invalidated purely based on a fixed time-to-live, regardless of content changes
explanation: Prompt caching keys on an exact, byte-for-byte prefix match at the start of the request; any change earlier in the sequence than the cached content breaks that match, which is why stable content (system prompt, tool definitions) should be placed first and variable content last to maximize cache-hit rate.

promptText: A staff engineer proposes eliminating conversation summarization entirely now that the company uses a 1M-token context model, reasoning 'we can just keep everything.' What is the strongest multi-faceted objection?
options: Summarization must never be relaxed regardless of window size, since any relaxation is unsafe

Unbounded raw history compounds cost and latency (quadratic-ish prefill growth per turn), doesn't fix lost-in-the-middle for buried early turns, and increases the blast radius of any context-leakage or injection issue by keeping more raw sensitive data resent every turn
1M-token models cannot process conversation history at all, only single documents
There is no valid objection; keeping full raw history is strictly better once the window is large enough
explanation: Full raw history means every turn re-processes an ever-larger, increasingly expensive prefill; lost-in-the-middle doesn't disappear at 1M tokens, so early turns aren't guaranteed to be reliably used even though present; and a larger retained raw history increases security exposure -- the right response is to relax the summarization threshold, not eliminate the discipline.

promptText: Two models both advertise a '128,000 token' context window but behave noticeably differently on the same long prompt. What best explains this?
options: One of the two models must be lying about its advertised window size

The advertised number is only the architectural maximum (how much technically fits), not a guarantee of effective context; models reach long lengths via different techniques (some trade attention fidelity for length via sparsity, others pay full quadratic cost), producing different 'lost in the middle' behavior even at identical advertised maximums
Context window size is purely a marketing number with no relationship to actual model behavior whatsoever
The difference can only be explained by one model using a slower GPU than the other
explanation: Techniques like sparse/windowed attention, RoPE-style positional encoding extensions, and full quadratic attention all reach long advertised windows through different trade-offs, so two models with identical advertised maximums can have measurably different effective context and different lost-in-the-middle curves -- benchmarking actual long-context behavior on your workload is necessary rather than trusting the marketing number.

promptText: A shared 'budget manager' library had a bug that dropped the reserved-output budget to zero under specific input shapes, silently causing truncated answers across multiple product teams. What is the correct staff-level structural fix, beyond just patching the bug?
options: Simply fix the one arithmetic bug and close the incident, since regression tests for that exact input are sufficient

Add a hard assertion in the shared library that fails loudly if the computed output reservation ever falls below a sane minimum floor, and add a metric tracking the actual output reservation applied per request so future regressions are caught by dashboard anomaly rather than accumulated complaints
Remove the shared library entirely and have every team hand-roll its own budgeting logic to reduce blast radius
Increase the model's context window size so budget errors become mathematically impossible
explanation: Because the bug lived in a shared library, the durable fix is structural: prevent the failure class from recurring silently (a hard floor assertion that fails loudly instead of allowing zero/negative reservations to pass through) and add instrumentation so any future regression of this shape surfaces immediately as a dashboard anomaly rather than through scattered customer complaints across teams.
